summary:
Skibidi toilet gets more attention from kids than the Moon does. Outpost 0 is our way of fighting back. 
Outpost 0 is an educational game that teaches children aged 7 to 12 about space through play. Players manage a space outpost and make decisions that have real consequences. Every choice, from rationing oxygen to repairing equipment, changes the base’s resources and safety, so players learn what it takes to survive and work in space.
Our game addresses the Junior Astronaut challenge by turning NASA data into events and scenarios that players face. Instead of reading facts, kids see how real space data shapes decisions, which makes the science easier to remember.
Many children find space and science hard to connect with. Outpost 0 gives them a safe, fun way to build curiosity, problem-solving skills and an understanding of life beyond Earth. We tested the game with our team member, 11 years old, in our target age group, and her feedback shaped its design.
details:
Outpost 0 is a 3D browser game for kids aged 7 to 12. The player is sent from Earth to save the crew of Outpost 0, a base on the Moon or Mars that was damaged by a solar storm. They start in Mission Control, pick the Moon or Mars, pack their rocket and fly there. On the base they keep three resources alive: Power, Shield and Air & Water. Problems come in over the radio, and each one is a short mini-game, like aiming solar panels, blocking radiation, cleaning water or drilling for ice. After each mission they get a real space fact, and at the end they fly the crew home. There’s also a short training mode with 3 levels.

The game runs on real NASA data. We use DONKI (https://ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/tools/DONKI/) for real solar flares, CMEs and geomagnetic storms: a bigger flare sends more radiation at the base, a faster CME gives less time to protect the solar panels, and a stronger storm adds more radio noise. We use NASA APIs (https://api.nasa.gov) for the Photo of the Day, Earth photos and asteroids passing Earth today. We use NASA EONET (https://eonet.gsfc.nasa.gov) to show real fires, storms and volcanoes on a map. Because the data is live, every game is a bit different.

What makes it different is that the NASA data isn’t just text on a screen, it changes the game itself. There are no multiple-choice tasks, so kids learn by doing. It also has a full story, from launch to rescue to coming home. Kids get a small alien buddy called Zee who shows them where to go, they can design their own astronaut and rocket, and they unlock new gear by learning.

Most space information is only available in English, so we built a full Arabic version with a talking commander, so kids in Egypt and the Arab world can learn in their own language. We kept everything simple for young kids, with short sentences, big buttons, and voice with subtitles. Every fact comes from a NASA or published source.

We built it with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, using Three.js (https://threejs.org) for the 3D. It runs in any browser with no install and is hosted on GitHub Pages. Moon radiation facts come from the Chang’e 4 study (Science Advances, 2020).

This is a working prototype. In the future we want to add more missions, more NASA data, and more languages so kids everywhere can learn about space.

We used Claude and Manus AI to help debug the game's code (HTML, CSS and JavaScript). Claude also translated the game into Arabic for the translation option. The idea, story, game design and testing with our 11-year-old team member are our own work. All AI-assisted code and text were reviewed by our team. No AI-generated images, video or audio are used in the game.
